tip: 'Dar com a língua nos dentes' is literally your tongue hitting your teeth, the moment a secret slips out and gets told.
Portuguese can't leave a preposition dangling at the end like English does. 'Referir-se' keeps its 'a' up front: 'a quem me refiro'.
Where English says "the fact that he was late", Portuguese uses an infinitive with its own subject: 'o fato de ele ter se atrasado'.
'Fora próspera' means "had been prosperous". This '-ra' form is literary; in speech you'd say 'tinha sido próspera' instead.
'Por mais que tentemos' means "no matter how hard we try". 'Por mais que' triggers the 'tentemos' verb form, not plain 'tentamos'.
After 'se' for a future possibility, Portuguese uses the future subjunctive 'quiserem', while English just keeps the plain present "want".
'Que' plus a subjunctive is a third-person command or wish: 'que se inscreva' means "let them register", or they should register.
'Pese' comes from 'pesar', to weigh, so 'em que pese' is roughly "however it may weigh", a frozen formal formula meaning despite.
'Cujo' means whose and agrees with the thing owned, not the owner: 'cujo' is masculine here because 'faturamento' is masculine.
'Herdara' is a one-word form of "had inherited". The '-ara' ending marks it, and it is mostly literary now.
'Refiro' needs the preposition 'a' ('referir-se a'), so it appears before 'qual' too, and 'a' plus 'a qual' contracts to 'à qual'.
'Quanto mais... mais' is the Portuguese equivalent of "the more... the more": 'quanto mais se analisa, mais complexo o problema parece'.
Put 'o' before an adjective to turn it into a noun: 'o barato' means the cheap thing or option.
'Marcara' is a one-word form of "had marked", equal to 'tinha marcado'. Rare in speech, common in writing.
'Se' (if) about the future uses the future subjunctive: 'se a chuva parar'. For regular verbs the form looks identical to the infinitive.
'Vira' here is a one-word form of "had seen", from 'ver'. Do not confuse it with 'virar', meaning to turn.
'Trouxer' is the future subjunctive of 'trazer' (to bring); its stem comes from the past form 'trouxe', not the infinitive.
After 'se' for a future condition, Portuguese uses the future subjunctive: 'se eu obtiver a aprovação' means "if I get approval".
'Cumpre' plus an infinitive is a formal set phrase with no subject: 'cumpre salientar' means "it should be pointed out".
Set off by commas mid-sentence, 'pois' means "therefore", not "because". It is a formal connector in academic writing.
'Boca fechada', a closed mouth, carries the lesson: keep quiet, no flies get in, and you stay out of trouble.
In 'faz-se mister', 'mister' means "necessary" and has nothing to do with the English title. It's archaic formal speak for "it is required".
Here 'só' means alone or by itself, not "only": 'uma andorinha só' is one swallow on its own.
'Cola' comes from 'colar', literally "to glue", but in school slang it means to cheat; 'a cola' is a crib sheet.
'Quem' as whoever takes a third-person singular verb: 'quem espera', never 'quem esperam'.
Mix with the 'porcos' (pigs) and you'll end up eating 'farelo' (bran): the proverb warns that bad company rubs off on you.
'À' merges the preposition 'a' with the feminine article 'a' before a feminine noun: 'tange à metodologia' (regarding the methodology).
'Infere-se' puts 'se' on the verb with no stated subject: "it is inferred" or "one infers". Standard in formal writing.
'Malgrado' means despite and attaches straight to a noun, with no 'de': 'malgrado as limitações' (despite the limitations).
'Visa analisar' means "aims to analyze". Both 'visa analisar' and 'visa a analisar' are accepted in academic writing.
